summary: Specifies how to use SIP to establish an SRTP security context using DTLS. It describes carrying a fingerprint attribute in SDP to bind the signaling to the DTLS handshake used on the media path. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: To protect a call, each side shares a fingerprint of its ID ahead of time. Later, when the secure connection begins, they can check it matches and know they are talking to the right person.

subtitle: How SIP calls agree on encryption keys over the media path by exchanging only certificate fingerprints in SDP.

tldr.problem: Encrypting a SIP call usually means putting keys in the signaling, which forces every proxy on the path to be trusted, or relying on certificates from a well-known authority.
tldr.mechanism: Each endpoint puts a fingerprint of its certificate in the SDP offer or answer. The endpoints then run a mutually authenticated DTLS handshake on the media path and check that each certificate matches the fingerprint received in signaling.
tldr.outcome: Keys never travel in SIP, and self-signed certificates are enough. The protection is only as strong as the integrity of the signaling, so SIP Identity or an equivalent is needed to stop active attackers. RFC 8842 later updated this framework.

today: RFC 5763 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8842, which replaces the common SDP offer/answer procedures with a reference to itself. No RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SIP and SDP set up multimedia calls, and RTP carries the real-time media. This RFC gives a framework for setting up SRTP security over UDP by using an extension to DTLS (defined in RFC 5764). The goal is a key negotiation technique that lets devices with no prior relationship talk encrypted, without trusting every signaling element on the route and without requiring certificates signed by a well-known authority.

The media runs over a mutually authenticated DTLS session where both sides have certificates. The RFC stresses that certificates are purely a carrier for public keys, because DTLS has no mode for bare keys. They can be self-signed and self-generated, and third-party certificates MAY be used if the peers have them. The fingerprints travel in SDP inside the SIP offer/answer exchange.

Unlike approaches that piggyback key exchange on signaling (such as MIKEY), DTLS-SRTP does the key exchange between the media endpoints and only cryptographically binds it to the SIP/SDP communication.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of passing secret keys through the post office, two friends agree on the secret face to face. The post office only carries a note describing what each friend's lock looks like.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.content:
Alice wants an encrypted audio session with Bob. She sends an SDP offer to Bob over SIP. When she uses self-signed certificates, the offer includes a fingerprint that binds the DTLS key exchange in the media plane to the signaling plane.

The fingerprint alone protects against active attacks on the media but not against active attacks on the signaling. To stop those, SIP Identity (RFC 4474) may be used. When Bob receives the offer, the peers set up one DTLS connection per media session with mutual authentication. Bob can check that Alice's certificate matches the fingerprint in her offer. When Bob answers with his own fingerprint, Alice can do the same. Each side then knows the media is going to the other party without needing global PKI certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice and Bob pass a note about their locks through a messenger, then meet to build the secret handshake. Each checks the other's lock against the note.

sections.title: Why a New Approach
sections.content:
Earlier work existed, such as SDP Security Descriptions and MIKEY-based key management. This RFC lists its own reasons for choosing DTLS:

  • TLS is well known and widely implemented, and many SIP endpoints already implement it.
  • Forking and early media work without requiring PRACK, while the offerer can still choose keying material.
  • Security is established along the media path, which in many deployments differs from the signaling path.
  • With RFC 4474 the scheme works even when proxies downstream of the authentication service are not trusted, and no keys appear in SIP or SDP.
  • SSRC collisions cause no extra SIP signaling.

Because only integrity of the signaling is needed, not confidentiality, far fewer elements need credentials and trust. By contrast, SDESCRIPTIONS requires confidential signaling, so every intermediate element must be trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the secret is made in private between the two friends, the people carrying notes in between do not have to be trusted with anything important.

sections.title: Establishing a Secure Channel
sections.content:
The offer includes the fingerprint of the certificate the offerer wants to use. The endpoint SHOULD send it to its SIP proxy over an integrity protected channel, and the proxy SHOULD add an Identity header field per RFC 4474. The Identity header is a digital signature over several SIP header fields and the message body, so the receiver can tell the message was not tampered with.

The offer and answer MUST follow these rules:

  • Use the setup attribute from RFC 4145. The offerer MUST use setup:actpass and be ready to receive a client_hello before the answer arrives. The answerer MUST use setup:active or setup:passive, and setup:active is RECOMMENDED because the DTLS handshake can then run in parallel with the answer.
  • Do not use the connection attribute from RFC 4145.
  • Use the certificate fingerprint attribute from RFC 4572.
  • The certificate presented in the DTLS handshake MUST match the fingerprint exchanged in SDP. If it does not, the endpoint MUST tear down the media session immediately.

Whichever party is active MUST start a DTLS handshake by sending a ClientHello over each flow. The offerer may only tentatively accept the answerer's certificate until it receives the answer with the answerer's fingerprint. Endpoints are not required to generate a new certificate for each session, since key generation is relatively expensive.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must show a lock that matches the note they sent earlier. If it does not match, they hang up right away.

sections.title: Calls, Forking and Other Situations
sections.content:
The RFC works through how the scheme behaves in common SIP situations.

  • Early media: an endpoint that wants to provide early media MUST take the setup:active role, and can start the DTLS association and send media at once. The passive side may not yet have validated the fingerprint.
  • Forking: each answerer forms its own DTLS association, and the offerer matches the fingerprint in each answer to the certificate of each association.
  • Rekeying: DTLS endpoints can rekey at any time by redoing the handshake, and keep using the old keys until the new ones are ready.
  • Session modification: peers may reuse existing associations if the fingerprints and transport parameters match; if the active or passive roles change, a new connection MUST be established.
  • ICE: all candidate pairs of one component are treated as the same DTLS association, so only one handshake happens.
  • No ICE: if the handshake has not finished when the passive side gets the other SDP, it MUST send one unauthenticated STUN check to open the NAT pinhole.
  • Anonymous calls: DTLS-SRTP does not give anonymity and may deanonymize an anonymous call unless a fresh self-signed certificate is used per call.

Implementations MUST support DTLS-SRTP (RFC 5764) and the SDP capability negotiation mechanism, so an offer can prefer SRTP while still offering plain RTP. A conference server cannot share one encryption context among participants, because each handshake creates fresh keys that neither side fully controls.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules cover odd cases, such as a call that rings several phones at once. Every phone that picks up makes its own secret with the caller, so nobody shares anyone else's secret.

sections.title: An Example Call
sections.content:
In the main example Alice calls Bob, and the two share a proxy. Alice sends her INVITE to her proxy over TLS, offering a=setup:actpass and a SHA-1 fingerprint computed from her self-signed certificate. The offer also lists plain RTP as a default in case the answerer does not support SRTP. The proxy adds Identity and Identity-Info headers and forwards it.

Bob chooses to be the DTLS client. He sends a ClientHello to Alice on her RTP port, and another for RTCP on the next port. Alice replies with her ServerHello and Certificate, and Bob finishes his side of the handshake. Bob can then send early media, but Alice cannot yet trust it because she has not received his fingerprint, and her user interface shows that lack of trusted media. When Bob answers, his 200 OK carries his fingerprint with a=setup:active. Alice validates the certificate and her endpoint shows the call as secured. Two further examples show connected identity with an UPDATE (RFC 4916) and a STUN check for the NAT case.
sections.plainLanguage: Bob starts building the secret before he picks up the phone. Alice cannot be sure it is really Bob until his note arrives, so her phone shows a warning. Once the note arrives and matches, the warning goes away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is frank about the limits. Without integrity protection of the signaling, security is limited to defense against passive attack by intermediaries; an active attack on both signaling and media can break the connection. Ways to protect the fingerprint include SIP Identity, S/MIME, and the weaker hop-by-hop SIPS, which only helps if all proxies are trusted.

SIP Identity does not sign responses, so the RFC describes using RFC 4916: Bob sends his answer and then an UPDATE carrying the fingerprint, asserted through his authentication service. Offerers SHOULD support this and answerers SHOULD use it. If Bob skips it, an attacker on the signaling path could swap his fingerprint and sit in the middle, though Bob would notice the attack.

Other points:

  • Continuity of authentication: implementations SHOULD keep a constant long-term key, cache each peer's key and alert the user if it changes.
  • Short Authentication String: people can read fingerprints aloud; the RFC says the minimal secure fingerprint length is around 64 bits.
  • Identity limits: the assurance is only as good as SIP Identity. A UA MUST NOT indicate a secure call to the claimed identity if a middlebox has broken the Identity signature.
  • Forward secrecy: DTLS supports Diffie-Hellman and Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman suites so a stolen long-term key does not expose past calls.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret is only as safe as the note that carries the lock description. If a sneaky messenger can change the note, the plan can be fooled, so the note should be sealed.
